metric_definitions.recall@k: gold chunks in the top k / gold chunks
metric_definitions.precision@k: gold chunks in the top k / k, even when fewer than k come back
metric_definitions.wrong_evidence: questions where a hard negative ranks above at least one gold chunk in the retrieved list (a gold chunk not retrieved ranks below all), or is cited anywhere in the raw answer / questions with hard negatives; by_relation counts a question under each hard-negative label that triggered, over the questions with a negative of that label; share_of_wrong is the share of wrong questions that label triggered (H3)
metric_definitions.exact_match: share of questions whose filter companies and periods both equal the labels
metric_definitions.companies_match: share of questions whose filter companies equal the tickers label
metric_definitions.periods_match: share of questions whose filter periods equal the fiscal_periods label
metric_definitions.filter_excluded_gold: gold chunks whose filing the filter excluded, summed over questions
metric_definitions.structural_citation_validity: cited chunk IDs that were among the retrieved chunks / cited chunk IDs, counted over every sentence of the raw answer, kept or dropped; null when nothing was cited
metric_definitions.dropped_share: sentences dropped by citation enforcement / sentences in the raw answers
metric_definitions.status: the answer's status line: answered, declined, not_found; no_status if the line was missing; refused if the API refused
metric_definitions.latency_ms: p50 and p95 per stage, by linear interpolation between the closest ranks; embed and retrieval (embed plus search) count only questions whose query embedding was made in this run; generation is each answer call's API latency when it was made, also for an answer replayed from the cache
metric_definitions.total_ms: the wall time of each question's whole arm call, p50 and p95 by linear interpolation over every question in the cell; replayed counts the questions with any call replayed from a cache (query embedding, answer, Cypher or map call), whose total is shorter than a fresh run's, and each such question record says replayed
metric_definitions.cost_usd: from the token counts each API reported and the header's dated price table; Voyage at list price, before any free allowance
metric_definitions.interval: percentile bootstrap 95% interval over 10000 resamples of the cell's questions, with replacement; each interval's generator is seeded by the header's seed and the interval's set, arm, class and metric; for a ratio, resamples with a zero denominator are left out and 'resamples' counts the rest
metric_definitions.directional: the cell has fewer than 10 questions in the scored split (research plan)
metric_definitions.judged: scored by an LLM judge, uncalibrated: no judge has been checked against hand scores yet; each metric runs 3 times as independent calls; a question's score is the mean of its runs that produced a value and its spread the highest run minus the lowest; a cell's mean is over its questions' scores, run_means is the cell mean within each run, spread is the highest run mean minus the lowest, and the interval resamples the questions' scores; a run with no value (skipped, undefined, or an unusable judge reply, which 'errors' counts) is left out
metric_definitions.faithfulness: Ragas faithfulness: statements in the kept sentences (citation markers removed) that the judge infers from the retrieved chunks / statements; skipped when no sentence was kept; no value when the judge finds no statements
metric_definitions.answer_relevancy: Ragas answer relevancy: mean cosine similarity (Voyage query embeddings) between the question and 3 questions the judge writes from the shown answer (citation markers removed), 0 if the judge calls every one noncommittal; skipped for an empty answer
metric_definitions.citation_support: kept sentences whose cited chunks, together, support every claim in them, per the judge / kept sentences; skipped when no sentence was kept
metric_definitions.judged_cost_usd: what judging cost (OpenAI judge calls plus Voyage embeddings for answer relevancy), over all runs; an evaluation cost, kept out of the operational cost_usd, which is what answering a question costs
metric_definitions.judge_usage: judge tokens over all runs as OpenAI reported them, replayed calls included: input_tokens includes cached_input_tokens and cache_write_tokens; output_tokens includes reasoning_tokens, which are shown separately and billed as output
metric_definitions.decline_correct: decline records: 1 if the judge finds the answer declined to advise
metric_definitions.not_found_correct: unanswerable records: 1 if the judge finds the answer said the filings lack the evidence without stating or guessing the fact
metric_definitions.graph: graph arms only: no_anchor counts questions that linked no anchor, empty_retrieval those whose retrieval held no chunk, not_found those answered not_found
metric_definitions.cypher_validity: graph_traversal only, per question: first_pass_valid when the first query passed the guard and ran without error in the timeout; valid_after_repair when the first or its one repair did; non_empty when one returned chunks; fallback when the question fell back to graph_local; null with no query
metric_definitions.graph_stages: anchor_linking, cypher_generation, cypher_repair and cypher_execution latency counts the questions that ran the stage; their cost is a mean over every question, a stage that did not run costing 0; search covers every stage after the query embedding; community_select and global_map latency counts the questions that ran the stage; global_map's is the map step's wall time, its tokens and cost summed over the map calls; their cost is a mean over every question, a stage that did not run costing 0; search covers every stage after the query embedding; the reduce call writes the answer, so its latency and cost are generation's
metric_definitions.global_search: graph_global only: map points are dropped when they cite no chunk, cite a chunk their call was not shown, or have no score from 0 to 100; the reduce call reads the kept points above 0 by score, then community rank, within reduce_budget_tokens (cl100k_base); with none, the answer is not_found and no reduce call is made, counted as no_reduce; map_calls_unusable counts map replies cut off, refused or off the schema, which give their community no points; no_community counts questions with no community selected; the reduce call writes the answer, so its cost and latency are generation's
metric_definitions.routing: the router's classifier call: its latency is the call's API latency when it was made (also when replayed) and its cost is in every question's total; a question the router declined makes no retrieval or answer call and is left out of the retrieval, embed, search and generation latency
metric_definitions.router: router runs only: each question record's routing holds the predicted class (lookup, local, multi_hop, global or decline), the classifier's reason, the routing map, the arm chosen (decline: the fixed decline sentence, with no retrieval and no answer call), the effort and prompt, and the classifier call's cost; the header's router.arms holds each arm the router opened, as that arm's own run records it
metric_definitions.mode: full: retrieval, answers and judges; retrieval_only: retrieval alone, with no answer or judge call, so cells hold retrieval metrics, retrieval latency and the wrong-evidence rate from ranks alone (nothing is cited), and no answer, judged, cost or total_ms fields

decline.note: no gold chunks; retrieval metrics do not apply

questions.question: Beyond lost direct sales, what knock-on competitive effects of U.S.-China export controls and trade tensions do NVIDIA, AMD and Intel describe in their latest 10-Ks?

answer.text:
NVIDIA says export controls have a disproportionate impact on it and may disadvantage it against competitors selling chips outside the controls' scope [0001045810-26-000021:0044][0001045810-26-000021:0045]. It says the controls have encouraged customers to "design-out" certain U.S. semiconductors, and overseas governments to ask customers to buy from competitors rather than NVIDIA [0001045810-26-000021:0045].
It says this helped competitors build larger developer and customer ecosystems to challenge it worldwide [0001045810-26-000021:0042][0001045810-26-000021:0014].
This pushes customers in China, the Middle East and elsewhere toward suppliers based in China, Europe and Israel [0001045810-26-000021:0043]. It also says its competitive position has been harmed and will be harmed further if restrictions persist or expand, if customers buy from competitors or develop internal solutions, or if licenses are delayed [0001045810-26-000021:0043].
It has also discouraged them from buying, importing or using NVIDIA data center products, including China-specific products designed to comply with U.S. rules [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. Chinese regulators published a preliminary finding on September 15, 2025 that NVIDIA's compliance with U.S. export controls violated the terms of China's approval of its Mellanox acquisition, which could bring penalties or restrictions [0001045810-26-000021:0015][0001045810-26-000021:0041].
Controls have hurt and may hurt demand in Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia, and may increase investment in foreign competitors less likely to be restricted [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. They can also disrupt supply chains and distribution channels, including for non-data-center products [0001045810-26-000021:0045][0001045810-26-000021:0041]. The possibility of further controls has already reduced demand, benefiting competitors with alternatives less likely to be restricted, and can leave NVIDIA with excess inventory and purchase obligations, as with the H20 [0001045810-26-000021:0041][0001045810-26-000021:0045].
NVIDIA also says possible U.S. restrictions on supporting applications and models built on China-originating open-source foundation models would favor foreign competitors [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. If U.S. controls were eased, China could modify or implement the plan so that NVIDIA cannot design products to meet it, which could materially and adversely affect its business [0001045810-26-000021:0045][0001045810-26-000021:0046].
AMD says U.S. export restrictions on semiconductors to China make it easier for China-based competitors to develop and sell their own solutions, reducing the need for AMD's products [0000002488-26-000018:0042]. Limits on China sales could hurt its competitive position against domestic Chinese competitors and others not subject to the same restrictions, so it could lose market position [0000002488-26-000018:0043].
Downstream recipients of its products can face added restrictions on use, resale, repair or transfer, and AMD may be at a disadvantage if competitors are not subject to the same restrictions [0000002488-26-000018:0044].
A U.S. government request for 15% of licensed MI308 China revenue could raise AMD's costs, harm its competitive position and benefit competitors not subject to such arrangements [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. Licenses may be temporary or carry onerous conditions, and without them AMD may be unable to develop a competitive China-market product [0000002488-26-000018:0043].
New export controls could affect R&D teams outside the U.S. that execute product roadmaps, and raise compliance costs for AMD and its customers [0000002488-26-000018:0044]. Replacement rules for the rescinded AI Diffusion Rule could disrupt key customer and supplier relationships and cost AMD competitive positioning in international markets [0000002488-26-000018:0043].
Retaliatory actions or policies promoting domestic products could further hurt its business, with possible inventory impairment charges [0000002488-26-000018:0044][0000002488-26-000018:0043].
It says China has responded with its own restrictions, including on critical minerals [0000050863-26-000011:0072]. It also says Chinese semiconductor companies such as SMIC are investing heavily, often with government support, to build products that compete with Intel's [0000050863-26-000011:0072].

STATUS: answered

The points say nothing about NVIDIA, so they cannot show how its climate and environmental-regulation risks compare with AMD's or Intel's. The comparison below covers only AMD (fabless) and Intel (runs its own fabs).

Intel's exposure is direct and tied to its own manufacturing. Environmental laws on materials, processes, air quality and wastewater may impede its ability to manufacture or expand manufacturing capability. They can also require pollution abatement or remediation equipment, product redesign, or ceasing use of a material or process [0000050863-26-000011:0087]. Intel says perfluorocarbons, historically a large portion of its direct greenhouse gas emissions, are used in semiconductor manufacturing. New limits could require abatement equipment, carbon offsets or altered production processes, and stricter climate regulation could raise manufacturing and energy costs, for example through carbon pricing on electrical utilities [0000050863-26-000011:0087]. Intel also says PFAS regulations could limit or prohibit their use in parts, process chemicals and materials. It says feasible alternatives are limited, and that expanding manufacturing capacity could magnify the impact of future laws [0000050863-26-000011:0087]. Its materials and chemicals are subject to broad environmental, health and safety laws, which apply to both its operations and its suppliers'. Violations or amended laws can bring penalties, fines, remediation obligations, suspension of production, altered manufacturing processes and restrictions on operations or sales [0000050863-26-000011:0086].

AMD, which is fabless, frames its risk around products, suppliers and customers. Its environmental laws cover materials used in its products and manufacturing processes, and its suppliers must obtain permits for operations such as air-pollutant and wastewater discharge. Compliance has no presently material adverse impact, but regulatory changes could have one in the future [0000002488-26-000018:0018]. AMD's climate risk centers on natural disasters that could disrupt energy or water, interrupt its supply chain, delay manufacturing and shipments, and raise costs, affecting its own, its suppliers' and its customers' operations [0000002488-26-000018:0040]. It also cites a demand-side risk: data centers depend on clean water and reliable energy, and customers who cannot secure sufficient power or water may reduce or stop purchases from AMD [0000002488-26-000018:0040][0000002488-26-000018:0041]. Its regulatory risk covers carbon taxes, greenhouse gas emission rules and fuel or energy taxes, which would likely raise costs through carbon pricing on utilities or required renewable energy purchases. AMD also expects costs to comply with climate disclosure requirements [0000002488-26-000018:0041].

AMD describes product-focused rules. These include restrictions on lead and other materials in electronic products in the EU and China, evolving PFAS chemical reporting, product energy-efficiency regulations in the EU, California and China, and e-waste and extended producer responsibility rules. The inconsistent scope of these laws increases compliance complexity [0000002488-26-000018:0019]. AMD has also been named a responsible party at three Superfund sites in Sunnyvale, California, tied to legacy releases from former underground tanks. It has recorded an estimated environmental liability of approximately $5.9 million (FY2025 10-K) and believes any additional amount would not be material [0000002488-26-000018:0018][0000002488-26-000018:0019].

points.text: AMD (FY2025 10-K) frames climate risk around its own and its suppliers' and customers' operations: natural disasters could disrupt energy or water, interrupt its supply chain, delay manufacturing and shipments, and raise costs to maintain or restore operations [0000002488-26-000018:0040].

AMD says its supply chain manufacturing suppliers may incur higher costs from new climate-related expectations (abatement equipment, renewable energy, changed production processes and materials), and those compliance costs may be passed on to AMD as greater indirect costs. This is the fabless-style, indirect exposure to environmental regulation.

AMD's climate-related regulatory risk covers carbon taxes, greenhouse gas emission rules and fuel or energy taxes, which would likely raise costs through carbon pricing on utilities or required renewable energy purchases. It also expects to incur costs to comply with new or proposed climate disclosure requirements, and failure to comply could bring enforcement, litigation or reputational harm [0000002488-26-000018:0041].

AMD highlights a demand-side climate risk: data centers depend on clean water and reliable energy, and if customers cannot secure sufficient power or water they may be unable to expand capacity and may reduce or stop purchases from AMD [0000002488-26-000018:0040][0000002488-26-000018:0041].

AMD notes that its insurance policies have large deductibles and broad exclusions, so losses not covered by insurance could be significant and materially harm its results. The excerpts say nothing about NVIDIA or Intel, so they cannot show how those companies' climate risks differ, including Intel's own-fab exposure [0000002488-26-000018:0041].

AMD (fabless) says its environmental laws cover materials used in its products and manufacturing processes, and that its suppliers must obtain permits for operations such as air-pollutant and wastewater discharge. Compliance has no presently material adverse impact, but changes to regulations could have one in the future [0000002488-26-000018:0018].

AMD has been named a responsible party at three Superfund sites in Sunnyvale, California on the National Priorities List, tied to legacy releases from former underground tanks. It has recorded an estimated environmental liability of approximately $5.9 million (FY2025 10-K) with no insurance recoveries recorded, and believes any additional amount would not be material [0000002488-26-000018:0018][0000002488-26-000018:0019].

AMD faces evolving product-related environmental rules: restrictions on lead and other materials (EU, China), PFAS chemical reporting, product energy-efficiency regulations for computers and servers, and e-waste/extended producer responsibility rules requiring labeling, fees or reporting. Their inconsistent scope increases compliance complexity, and AMD cannot assure that they won't require significant costs or product design changes [0000002488-26-000018:0019].

Under the Superfund Act, current and previous owners or operators of real property can face strict, and in some cases joint and several, liability for cleanup costs even if they did not know of the release. AMD's remaining responsibility includes on-site cleanup and costs not covered by its agreement with another responsible party at one site [0000002488-26-000018:0018][0000002488-26-000018:0019].

AMD (FY2025 10-K) says it has been responsible for Superfund cleanup, has recorded an estimated environmental liability of approximately $5.9 million for anticipated future remediation costs under the orders, and believes any additional amount would not be material; another responsible party covers certain offsite cleanup under one agreement, while AMD remains responsible for on-site cleanup and for all remaining costs if that party defaults [0000002488-26-000018:0019].

AMD (FY2025 10-K) describes product-focused environmental rules: restrictions on lead and other materials in electronic products in the EU and China, evolving PFAS chemical reporting, product energy-efficiency regulations in the EU, California and China, and e-waste and extended producer responsibility rules. It says the inconsistent scope of these laws increases compliance complexity [0000002488-26-000018:0019].

AMD says compliance has not historically had a material impact on its financial condition, earnings or competitive position. It cautions that evolving laws could still require significant costs, changes to operations or product designs, or other compliance actions [0000002488-26-000018:0019].

Intel, which runs its own fabs, says environmental laws on materials, processes, air quality and wastewater may impede its ability to manufacture or expand manufacturing capability, and can require pollution abatement or remediation equipment, product redesign, or ceasing use of a material or process [0000050863-26-000011:0087].

Intel says semiconductor manufacturing uses perfluorocarbons, historically a large portion of its direct greenhouse gas emissions, and that new limits could require abatement equipment, carbon offsets or altered production processes. It also says stricter climate regulation could raise manufacturing and energy costs, for example through carbon pricing on electrical utilities [0000050863-26-000011:0087].

Intel says regulations on PFAS, which are found in parts, process chemicals and materials used in semiconductor manufacturing, could limit or prohibit their use. It says there are limited feasible alternatives and that expanding manufacturing capacity could magnify the impact of future laws [0000050863-26-000011:0087].

Intel says its design, manufacturing, assembly and test require materials and chemicals subject to broad environmental, health and safety laws, which apply to both its operations and its suppliers'. Violations or amended laws can bring penalties, fines, remediation obligations, suspension of production, altered manufacturing processes and restrictions on operations or sales [0000050863-26-000011:0086].

Intel notes that some of its products, such as IPUs and certain Core Ultra versions, are made by an external foundry rather than Intel Foundry, depending on the product. Even so, it describes its own manufacturing exposure to environmental regulation as direct, which is the contrast with fabless peers [0000050863-26-000011:0017][0000050863-26-000011:0014].

questions.question: How does the share price shape the talent-retention risk that NVIDIA, AMD and Intel each describe in their latest 10-K risk factors?

answer.text:
For NVIDIA, the FY2026 10-K says that in times of stock price volatility, as it has experienced in the past and may experience in the future, the retentive value of its stock-based compensation may decrease [0001045810-26-000021:0037]. NVIDIA also says that competition for skilled talent drives up costs in the form of cash and stock-based compensation, and that it is highly dependent on its longstanding executive team [0001045810-26-000021:0037]. NVIDIA links its stock price to its operating results as well: missing the expectations of investors or analysts is likely to cause its stock price to decline or become substantially volatile, and that volatility is the condition under which it says stock-based compensation loses retentive value [0001045810-26-000021:0038][0001045810-26-000021:0037].
The excerpts cover only NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K and contain no risk-factor language from either company on how share price affects talent retention, so no comparison can be drawn [0001045810-26-000021:0037].

questions.question: How did AI accelerator demand show up in each company's segment results in its latest 10-K, and what accelerator-related inventory charges offset it?

answer.text:
NVIDIA's Data Center revenue for fiscal year 2026 was up 68% from a year ago, driven by accelerated computing and AI [0001045810-26-000021:0063]. Its Compute & Networking segment revenue rose 67% to $193,479 million, and segment operating income rose 57% to $130,141 million [0001045810-26-000021:0066]. Within that, Data Center computing revenue grew 59% on demand for Blackwell, and Data Center networking revenue grew 142% [0001045810-26-000021:0066]. Offsetting this, NVIDIA took a $4.5 billion charge in the first quarter of fiscal 2026 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations, after a U.S. government license requirement for H20 exports to China reduced demand [0001045810-26-000021:0014]. That charge also contributed to gross margin falling from 75.0% to 71.1% [0001045810-26-000021:0063].
AMD's Data Center net revenue was $16.6 billion in 2025, up 32%, primarily on demand for 5th generation EPYC processors and Instinct MI350 Series GPUs [0000002488-26-000018:0070]. Data Center operating income was $3.6 billion versus $3.5 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. The increase was held back by about $440 million of net inventory and related charges tied to the U.S. government export control on Instinct MI308 Data Center GPU products, along with higher cost of sales and operating expenses [0000002488-26-000018:0077].
For Intel, the DCAI segment, which includes AI accelerators among its offerings, had 2025 revenue of $16,919 million versus $16,125 million in 2024 [0000050863-26-000011:0035]. DCAI operating income rose to $3,422 million from $1,414 million [0000050863-26-000011:0035]. Intel attributes the 5% DCAI revenue increase to higher server revenue from hyperscale customer demand and higher networking-related product revenue, not specifically to accelerators [0000050863-26-000011:0042]. DCAI revenue in Q4 2025 was limited by wafer fabrication supply constraints, primarily on Intel 7 and Intel 3 [0000050863-26-000011:0042].

MATCH (co:Company)-[:FILED]->(f:Filing)
WHERE f.accession_no IN ['0000002488-26-000018','0000050863-26-000011','0001045810-26-000021']

 (toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'revenue' AND (toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'data center' OR toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'compute' OR toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'networking' OR toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'instinct' OR toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'gpu' OR toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'ai'))

 OR toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'writedown'
 OR toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'provision'
 OR toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'h20'
 OR toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'mi308'
 OR toLower(m.concept) CONTAINS 'accelerator'
)

questions.question: How do NVIDIA, AMD and Intel each address the OECD Pillar Two global minimum tax in their latest 10-Ks, and has any of them quantified its impact?

answer.text:
Pillar Two imposes a minimum effective corporate tax rate, and NVIDIA says its tax obligations and effective tax rate could increase as a result [0001045810-26-000021:0051]. It says a number of countries where it does business have enacted, or are enacting, elements of Pillar Two, including the recently released "side-by-side" framework with additional safe harbors and coordination mechanisms [0001045810-26-000021:0051]. It says Pillar Two changes, including those related to the side-by-side framework, may increase tax uncertainty and compliance costs and adversely affect its provision for income taxes, cash tax payments, results of operations and financial condition [0001045810-26-000021:0052][0001045810-26-000021:0051]. The excerpts give no dollar or percentage estimate, so NVIDIA has not quantified the impact there [0001045810-26-000021:0052].
AMD: Its FY2025 10-K says the impact of Pillar Two for 2024 and 2025 was immaterial, which is a qualitative assessment and not a dollar figure [0000002488-26-000018:0079]. Many countries have enacted Pillar Two-based laws effective from 2024, though some jurisdictions where AMD operates have not yet adopted them [0000002488-26-000018:0079]. It says it continues to evaluate the effect of proposed and enacted changes on its effective tax rate and cash flows [0000002488-26-000018:0079]. AMD calls these rules generally favorable but says each country must adopt them before they are enacted for financial accounting purposes [0000002488-26-000018:0046][0000002488-26-000018:0079]. In its risk factors, AMD lists Pillar One and Pillar Two among OECD discussions that could change tax rules and materially affect its tax obligations and effective tax rate [0000002488-26-000018:0046][0000002488-26-000018:0047].
AMD describes the impact as immaterial for 2024 and 2025 [0000002488-26-000018:0079], and NVIDIA gives no estimate [0001045810-26-000021:0052].

questions.question: How does dependence on external foundries, and on TSMC in particular, differ across NVIDIA, AMD and Intel according to their latest 10-K risk factors?

answer.text:
It relies on TSMC for all microprocessor and GPU wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes and primarily on GF for larger nodes [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. AMD says it is focusing its 7 nm and lower microprocessor and GPU portfolio on TSMC's processes, and that its business could be materially adversely affected if TSMC cannot make enough wafers at those nodes to meet demand [0000002488-26-000018:0032]. It also says TSMC manufactures its newest IC products, and that it relies on TSMC, UMC and its other foundries [0000002488-26-000018:0032]. AMD warns that foundry yield problems or delayed transitions to advanced process technologies could raise unit costs, hurt gross margin or force it to allocate supply among customers [0000002488-26-000018:0032]. Some manufacturing suppliers have no long-term commitment contracts and work on a purchase-order basis, and they could prioritize other customers, raise prices on short notice, require prepayments or cut deliveries [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. AMD's GF wafer supply agreement sets a minimum annual capacity allocation and pricing through 2026, with excess inventory or higher unit cost risk if its wafer needs fall below the purchase target [0000002488-26-000018:0030].
Intel mostly manufactures in its own fabs but also uses third-party foundries, including TSMC, which it calls a key foundry competitor [0000050863-26-000011:0018]. Some of its most advanced current and future products are made exclusively by TSMC or depend on critical TSMC-made components, including various compute die [0000050863-26-000011:0076][0000050863-26-000011:0075]. It could not finish products needing TSMC tiles until it designed and sourced replacement tiles, which would likely mean a substantial delay [0000050863-26-000011:0063][0000050863-26-000011:0075]. It also says it has less control over delivery schedules, yields, quality and costs for third-party-made products, and that insufficient foundry capacity could prevent it from meeting demand [0000050863-26-000011:0075]. Intel has long-term purchase commitments and large prepayments for foundry capacity, which may not meet its needs or be fully recoverable [0000050863-26-000011:0075][0000050863-26-000011:0074]. It also flags Taiwan concentration, since many products depend on Taiwan suppliers for critical components, including compute die, that cannot be easily or quickly replaced [0000050863-26-000011:0073]. Unlike AMD, Intel is itself a manufacturer through Intel Foundry, so its risk mixes its own fabs, reliance on ASML as sole EUV tool supplier, and dependence on TSMC for some advanced products [0000050863-26-000011:0023][0000050863-26-000011:0075].
The NVIDIA excerpt covers cybersecurity risk from reliance on third-party suppliers for critical business systems and does not name TSMC or any foundry [0001045810-26-000021:0030].

It relies on TSMC for all microprocessor and GPU wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes and primarily on GF for larger nodes, and says that if TSMC cannot make enough wafers at 7 nm or smaller, its business could be materially adversely affected [0000002488-26-000018:0029].

AMD's risk factors say some manufacturing suppliers have no long-term commitment contracts and work on a purchase-order basis. These suppliers also serve competitors and could prioritize other customers, raise prices on short notice, require prepayments or cut deliveries. AMD has a GF wafer supply agreement with a minimum annual capacity allocation and pricing through 2026, with excess inventory risk if its wafer needs fall short of the purchase target [0000002488-26-000018:0029].

AMD is focusing its 7 nm and lower microprocessor and GPU portfolio on TSMC's processes, and TSMC makes its newest IC products. It warns that foundry yield problems or delayed transitions to advanced process technologies could raise unit costs, hurt gross margin or force it to allocate supply among customers [0000002488-26-000018:0032].

Intel mostly manufactures in its own fabs but also uses third-party foundries, including TSMC, which it calls a key foundry competitor. Some of its most advanced current and future products are made exclusively by TSMC or depend on TSMC-made compute die, and it expects to keep using TSMC and other foundries for key tiles [0000050863-26-000011:0018][0000050863-26-000011:0075].

Intel's risk factors say its disaggregated tile design makes it exposed to TSMC supply interruptions, including from a dispute. It could not finish products needing TSMC tiles until it designed and sourced replacement tiles, which would likely mean a substantial delay. Intel also says it has less control over delivery schedules, yields, quality and costs for third-party-made products, and has long-term purchase commitments and large prepayments for foundry capacity [0000050863-26-000011:0063][0000050863-26-000011:0075].

AMD says it is presently focusing its 7 nm and lower microprocessor and GPU portfolio on TSMC's processes, and that if TSMC cannot make wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes in sufficient quantities to meet demand, its business could be materially adversely affected (FY2025 10-K) [0000002488-26-000018:0032].

AMD states that it relies on TSMC, UMC and its other foundries to produce wafers for its IC products, and that TSMC manufactures its newest IC products. The foundries must be able to move to advanced process technologies and larger wafer sizes, produce wafers at acceptable yields and deliver them on time (FY2025 10-K) [0000002488-26-000018:0032].

AMD says its third-party manufacturers are responsible for the process technologies used to fabricate its wafers, and that low yields can come from design, packaging or process technology failures. Lower yields would raise per-unit costs, hurt gross margin and could force AMD to allocate reduced supply among customers [0000002488-26-000018:0032].

AMD has a wafer supply agreement with GF that sets a minimum annual capacity allocation and pricing through 2026. If AMD's wafer needs fall below the annual purchase target, it could carry excess inventory or higher unit costs [0000002488-26-000018:0030].

AMD lists other foundry-dependence risks: limited control over delivery schedules, yield, cycle times and pricing; supply disruption at manufacturers or their subcontractors; and delays or lower yields if production moves to new manufacturers. It also reports an inventory loss in Q1 2024 from an incident at a contract manufacturer, and relies on ATMP joint ventures for the majority of its ATMP services [0000002488-26-000018:0030].

NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K says it relies on third-party suppliers for critical business systems such as cloud infrastructure, encryption and authentication, and email, which exposes it to supply-chain attacks or other disruptions, and it cannot guarantee that third parties in its supply chain or its partners' supply chains have not been compromised [0001045810-26-000021:0030].

NVIDIA also says it has limited insight into, and limited ability to monitor, its third-party suppliers' security practices, and that its response may be more difficult if a supplier suffers a security incident, which it says has happened in the past [0001045810-26-000021:0030].

This excerpt covers cybersecurity risk in NVIDIA's supply chain and does not name TSMC or any foundry, and it says nothing about AMD or Intel, so it cannot support a comparison of foundry or TSMC dependence across the three companies [0001045810-26-000021:0030].

Intel (FY2025 10-K) says it uses third-party foundries and expects to keep relying on them, and that it has less control over delivery schedules, yields, quality, quantities and costs for products made by third parties; insufficient foundry capacity could prevent it from meeting demand.[0000050863-26-000011:0075]

Intel (FY2025 10-K) says a limited number of third-party foundries offer leading-edge processes and are geographically concentrated in Asia. Some of its most advanced current and future products are or will be either exclusively manufactured by TSMC or reliant on critical TSMC-made components, including various compute die.[0000050863-26-000011:0076][0000050863-26-000011:0075]

Intel (FY2025 10-K) flags Taiwan concentration: many products depend on Taiwan suppliers for critical components, including compute die, that cannot be easily or quickly replaced, and other products are made entirely in Taiwan. Any disruption affecting Taiwan could significantly harm Intel's ability to obtain components and supply customers.[0000050863-26-000011:0073]

Intel (FY2025 10-K) is also a manufacturer itself, with its Intel Foundry business making CPUs alongside other suppliers. Its foundry-related risk is therefore a mix: it has its own fabs, relies on ASML as the sole EUV tool supplier, and also depends on TSMC for some advanced products.[0000050863-26-000011:0023][0000050863-26-000011:0075]

Intel (FY2025 10-K) has entered into long-term purchase commitments and large prepayments to secure substrates and third-party foundry capacity. These may not meet its needs, suppliers may fail to deliver, and prepayments may not be fully recoverable if demand falls short. It is currently affected by industry supply constraints for memory chips, substrates and foundry capacity.[0000050863-26-000011:0075][0000050863-26-000011:0074]

questions.question: How concentrated is each company's revenue among its largest customers, as disclosed in the latest 10-K risk factors of NVIDIA, AMD and Intel?

answer.text:
NVIDIA: In fiscal year 2026, one direct customer accounted for 22% of total revenue and another for 14%, both primarily attributable to the Compute & Networking segment [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. NVIDIA says it has had periods of getting a significant amount of revenue from a limited number of customers and that this may continue [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. It also generates a significant amount of revenue from a limited number of indirect customers, buying through OEMs, ODMs, system integrators and distributors, and it estimates some individually represent 10% or more of revenue [0001045810-26-000021:0036][0001045810-26-000021:0067]. In earlier years, one direct customer was 12% of revenue and two others were 11% each in fiscal 2025, and one direct customer was 13% in fiscal 2024 [0001045810-26-000021:0125][0001045810-26-000021:0067]. Most sales are on a purchase order basis, so customers can generally cancel, change or delay commitments with little notice and without penalty [0001045810-26-000021:0036].
Intel: Its three largest customers together accounted for 43% of net revenue in 2025, 45% in 2024 and 40% in 2023 [0000050863-26-000011:0083]. Losing key customers, a substantial drop in sales to them, or changes in their order timing could reduce revenue and increase volatility in results [0000050863-26-000011:0083][0000050863-26-000011:0084]. It also says industry trends such as growing AI workloads and the shift of data center workloads to the public cloud have increased the purchasing power of certain customers, particularly hyperscalers, in some data center-focused businesses [0000050863-26-000011:0084].
They say only that the success of its semi-custom SoC products in Client and Gaming depends on securing semi-custom customers and on the success of game consoles for Sony and Microsoft [0000002488-26-000018:0024]. They also describe AMD's Data Center customers as primarily hyperscale data centers, OEMs, ODMs, system integrators and distributors [0000002488-26-000018:0012].

questions.question: How do NVIDIA, AMD and Intel each describe the role of their software and developer ecosystems in competing for AI and computing workloads, according to their latest 10-Ks?

answer.text:
NVIDIA: NVIDIA cites an ecosystem of over 7.5 million developers using CUDA and its other software tools, and says its large and growing developer base and installed base strengthen the ecosystem and raise the platform's value to customers [0001045810-26-000021:0009][0001045810-26-000021:0004][0001045810-26-000021:0005]. It says more than half of its engineers work on software [0001045810-26-000021:0009][0001045810-26-000021:0004][0001045810-26-000021:0005]. Its full-stack platform rests on CUDA, introduced in 2006 to open its GPUs' parallel processing to compute-intensive applications, and on hundreds of domain-specific libraries, frameworks, SDKs and APIs [0001045810-26-000021:0004][0001045810-26-000021:0005]. NVIDIA lists software support and conformity to industry standard APIs among the principal competitive factors in its market, alongside performance, breadth of product offerings, access to customers, partners and distribution channels, and total system costs [0001045810-26-000021:0012]. Its Data Center systems combine GPUs, CPUs and interconnects with optimized AI and HPC software stacks, plus acceleration libraries, AI models, training data sets, APIs, SDKs and application frameworks [0001045810-26-000021:0006]. NVIDIA also sells software on top of its hardware, including NVIDIA AI Enterprise (which bundles NIM, NeMo and AI Blueprints), vGPU software, and industry stacks such as DRIVE, Omniverse and Clara [0001045810-26-000021:0009][0001045810-26-000021:0007][0001045810-26-000021:0005]. It further engages the open-model ecosystem and developers by releasing open AI models, running the Inception program with tens of thousands of startups, partnering with hundreds of universities, and offering NVLink Fusion so custom CPU and XPU designers can connect to its platform [0001045810-26-000021:0007][0001045810-26-000021:0009][0001045810-26-000021:0010]. Its Compute & Networking segment explicitly includes AI solutions and software [0001045810-26-000021:0123].
AMD: AMD says product competitiveness depends on factors including software and hardware compatibility, ease of use and functionality of software design tools, completeness of software solutions, and adherence to and creation of open industry standards [0000002488-26-000018:0014]. It develops software stacks of development tools, compilers and drivers for its CPUs, APUs, GPUs and FPGAs [0000002488-26-000018:0004]. It describes a comprehensive, open AI software stack supporting diverse AI ecosystems across frameworks, large and small language models and applications, positioned as part of full-stack solutions alongside its AI-optimized CPUs, GPUs and networking [0000002488-26-000018:0004].
Intel: Intel says x86 client CPUs are the foundational PC platform, which has enabled a deep and extensive software ecosystem [0000050863-26-000011:0011]. It says system-level integration of hardware and software will remain essential, and it plans to invest in heterogeneous compute, networking, memory and open standards so AI can be deployed at scale [0000050863-26-000011:0011]. In its risk factors, Intel says competitors' architectures such as ARM can produce beneficial network effects as an ecosystem of customers and application developers grows, and that ARM-based products and the ARM ecosystem have seen increased development and adoption [0000050863-26-000011:0059]. Intel defines oneAPI as an open, cross-architecture programming model allowing a single code base across multiple architectures, though the excerpt does not describe its competitive role [0000050863-26-000011:0180]. Its commercial CPU offerings, including the vPro Platform, come with an enterprise-grade software stack, and it is working with partners to enable new AI software capabilities on PCs in the enterprise [0000050863-26-000011:0014].

questions.question: According to NVIDIA's FY2026 10-K, how have U.S. export controls affected demand for NVIDIA products outside China, and what has the Chinese government done to discourage purchases of its data center products?

answer.text:
Outside China: The 10-K says export controls have in the past and may in the future negatively impact demand for NVIDIA's products and services not only in China but also in markets such as Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. It says the possibility of additional export controls has negatively impacted, and may in the future negatively impact, demand for its products, benefiting competitors that offer alternatives less likely to be restricted [0001045810-26-000021:0041]. Export controls have already encouraged, and may continue to encourage, customers outside China and other impacted regions to "design-out" certain U.S. semiconductors from their products [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. They have also encouraged overseas governments to ask NVIDIA's customers to buy from competitors rather than NVIDIA or other U.S. firms [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. The licensing requirements may encourage customers in China, the Middle East, and other regions to pursue alternatives, including semiconductor suppliers based in China, Europe, and Israel [0001045810-26-000021:0043]. Export controls can also disrupt NVIDIA's supply chain and distribution channels, hurting its ability to serve demand in markets outside China and for its non-data center products [0001045810-26-000021:0041]. Restrictions on data center GPUs may also reduce demand for NVIDIA's networking products used in servers containing those GPUs [0001045810-26-000021:0044]. Reduced demand due to export controls has led and could lead to excess inventory or related supply charges [0001045810-26-000021:0041].
Chinese government actions: The Chinese government has encouraged customers to purchase from China-based competitors and discouraged them from purchasing, importing, or using NVIDIA's data center products, including any China-specific product designed to comply with U.S. export controls [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. After U.S. legislative proposals calling for mandatory features in NVIDIA's chips, China's government publicly questioned whether the H20 products have built-in vulnerabilities, discouraging customers from purchasing them [0001045810-26-000021:0044]. An agency of the Chinese government announced an Action Plan endorsing new standards on compute performance per watt and per memory bandwidth for accelerators in new and renovated data centers, which could restrict customers' use of some NVIDIA data center products if NVIDIA returned to the market [0001045810-26-000021:0045]. On September 15, 2025, China's antitrust regulators published a preliminary finding that NVIDIA's compliance with U.S. export controls, which required offering degraded products to the Chinese market, discriminated unfairly against customers in China and violated the terms of China's approval of the Mellanox acquisition [0001045810-26-000021:0041].

questions.question: What is the status of NVIDIA's licensed H20 and H200 sales to China as described in its FY2026 10-K, including the financial impact and conditions attached to the licenses?

answer.text:
In April 2025, the USG informed NVIDIA that it requires a license for export to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and D:5 countries, or to companies headquartered or with an ultimate parent therein, of its H20 integrated circuits and any other circuits achieving the H20's memory bandwidth, interconnect bandwidth, or combination thereof [0001045810-26-000021:0042]. As a result, NVIDIA incurred a $4.5 billion charge in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026 associated with H20 for excess inventory and purchase obligations, as demand for H20 products diminished [0001045810-26-000021:0042][0001045810-26-000021:0061].
In August 2025, the USG granted licenses that would allow NVIDIA to ship certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, and NVIDIA generated approximately $60 million in H20 revenue under those licenses [0001045810-26-000021:0042][0001045810-26-000021:0061]. USG officials expressed an expectation that the USG will receive 15% or more of the revenue generated from licensed sales of NVIDIA's products, but the USG did not publish a regulation codifying such requirement [0001045810-26-000021:0042].
In February 2026, the USG granted a license that would allow NVIDIA to ship small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers [0001045810-26-000021:0042]. To date, NVIDIA has not generated any revenue under the H200 licensing program and does not yet know whether any imports will be allowed into China [0001045810-26-000021:0042][0001045810-26-000021:0061]. The license requires that the H200s go through an inspection process in the United States prior to any shipment to the customer, so any H200 shipped under the program will be subject to a 25% tariff upon importation into the United States [0001045810-26-000021:0042][0001045810-26-000021:0061].
If NVIDIA is able to sell licensed products into the China market, it may not be able to pass along all or any of the tariff to its customers, and may be subject to litigation, increased costs, and a harmed competitive position [0001045810-26-000021:0042]. NVIDIA also states that, as of the end of fiscal year 2026, it was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data center computing market [0001045810-26-000021:0042].

questions.question: How concentrated was NVIDIA's revenue among direct customers in fiscal year 2026, and what risks does NVIDIA associate with that concentration?

answer.text:
For fiscal year 2026, sales to one direct customer represented 22% of NVIDIA's total revenue and sales to another direct customer represented 14%, all of which were primarily attributable to the Compute & Networking segment [0001045810-26-000021:0067][0001045810-26-000021:0125]. In fiscal year 2025, one direct customer represented 12% of total revenue and two others each represented 11%, and in fiscal year 2024 one direct customer represented 13% [0001045810-26-000021:0067]. NVIDIA states that its revenue is concentrated among a limited number of direct and indirect customers and that this trend may continue [0001045810-26-000021:0067].
On indirect customers, NVIDIA says it generates a significant amount of revenue from a limited number of them, some individually representing 10% or more of revenue [0001045810-26-000021:0036].
The risk factor says revenue could be adversely affected if NVIDIA loses or is prevented from selling to any of these customers [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. Most sales are made on a purchase order basis, so customers can generally cancel, change or delay purchase commitments with little notice and without penalty [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. Partners or customers may buy fewer products, decline to incorporate NVIDIA's products into their ecosystem, develop their own solutions, or buy from competitors [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. NVIDIA also notes that a small number of partners are involved in system integration with its key customers, and that as system designs grow more complex, system integrators may be unable to meet key customers' specifications [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. If end demand rises or finished goods supply is concentrated near a quarter end, system integrators, distributors and channel partners may have limited ability to increase their credit, which could affect the timing and amount of revenue [0001045810-26-000021:0036]. Finally, NVIDIA says that the loss of any large customer, a significant reduction in their purchases, an inability to sell to a customer because of U.S. or other countries' trade restrictions, or difficulties collecting accounts receivable would likely harm its financial condition and results of operations [0001045810-26-000021:0036].

questions.question: In its Q3 fiscal 2026 10-Q, how does NVIDIA say export controls could affect its gaming and networking products beyond data center GPUs?

answer.text:
On gaming, NVIDIA says the USG already imposed export controls restricting certain gaming GPUs, and that expanding them to additional gaming products may disrupt a significant portion of its supply and distribution chain and negatively impact sales of such products to markets outside China, including the U.S. and Europe [0001045810-25-000230:0063]. It adds that as gaming GPU performance increases over time, export controls may have a greater impact on its ability to compete in markets subject to those controls [0001045810-25-000230:0063]. It also notes that export controls may disrupt the supply and distribution chain for a substantial portion of its products, which are warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong [0001045810-25-000230:0063]. Separately, it says export controls have disrupted and could in the future disrupt its supply chain and distribution channels, affecting its ability to serve demand in markets outside China and for its non-data center products [0001045810-25-000230:0059]. Restrictions by the Chinese government on the duration of gaming activities and access to games may also adversely affect Gaming revenue [0001045810-25-000230:0064].
On networking, NVIDIA says export controls restricting its ability to sell data center GPUs may also negatively impact demand for its networking products used in servers containing its GPUs [0001045810-25-000230:0063]. It says the USG may also impose export controls on networking products, such as high-speed network interconnects, to limit the ability of downstream parties to create large clusters for frontier model training [0001045810-25-000230:0063]. In addition, China's antitrust regulators published a preliminary finding on September 15, 2025 that NVIDIA's compliance with U.S. export controls violated the terms of China's approval of the Mellanox acquisition, and if regulators conclude NVIDIA failed to fulfill those terms, it could face restrictions or other orders regarding its networking business, products, and services [0001045810-25-000230:0060].

questions.question: How did the April 2025 U.S. export license requirement affect AMD's MI308 business over fiscal 2025, according to AMD's FY2025 10-K?

answer.text: In April 2025, the U.S. government implemented a new license requirement for the export of certain semiconductor products to a D5 Country and to companies headquartered in, or with an ultimate parent in, such a country, and this restriction impacts AMD's Instinct MI308 products [0000002488-26-000018:0042]. As a result, AMD incurred approximately $800 million in inventory and related charges in the second quarter of 2025 [0000002488-26-000018:0042][0000002488-26-000018:0072]. AMD applied for and was granted some licenses that allow it to ship MI308 products to certain China-based customers [0000002488-26-000018:0042]. During the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, AMD began shipping products and reversed approximately $360 million of the charges recorded earlier in the year [0000002488-26-000018:0042][0000002488-26-000018:0072]. The net effect for the year was approximately $440 million of net inventory and related charges associated with the export control on MI308 products, which partially offset the gross margin improvement to 50% from 49% in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0070][0000002488-26-000018:0078]. The same $440 million of net charges also partially offset the increase in Data Center operating income, which was $3.6 billion in 2025 versus $3.5 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. AMD states that sales of MI308 products into China depend on customer demand, China's import control rules and its ability to obtain licenses [0000002488-26-000018:0042]. In August 2025, U.S. government officials expressed an expectation that the U.S. government will receive 15% of the revenue from licensed MI308 sales to China, but the government has not published a regulation establishing such a requirement [0000002488-26-000018:0042][0000002488-26-000018:0072].

questions.question: Which manufacturers does AMD rely on to produce its products, per its FY2025 10-K, and what supply risks does it describe from that reliance?

answer.text:
AMD uses third-party wafer foundries to fabricate the silicon wafers for all of its products [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. It relies on TSMC for all wafers for microprocessor and GPU products at 7 nm or smaller nodes, and primarily on GLOBALFOUNDRIES (GF) for microprocessor and GPU wafers at process nodes larger than 7 nm [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. It also uses TSMC, UMC and Samsung for its programmable logic device ICs [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. Third-party manufacturers assemble, test, mark and pack (ATMP) its products, and most ATMP services come from two ATMP joint ventures with affiliates of Tongfu Microelectronics Co., Ltd. [0000002488-26-000018:0029][0000002488-26-000018:0030].
- If it experiences supply constraints, AMD may have to allocate reduced quantities among customers, which could harm customer relationships and its financial condition [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. Late or fluctuating supply could cause lost sales [0000002488-26-000018:0029].
- If TSMC cannot make enough wafers at 7 nm or smaller nodes to meet demand, its business could be materially adversely affected [0000002488-26-000018:0029].
- AMD does not have long-term commitment contracts with some manufacturing suppliers, and obtains many services by purchase order with no minimum quantity beyond existing orders [0000002488-26-000018:0029]. questions.question: What drove AMD's Data Center segment revenue and operating income in 2025, according to its FY2025 10-K MD&A?

answer.text:
Data Center net revenue was $16.6 billion in 2025, up 32% from $12.6 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. The increase was primarily driven by strong demand for AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct GPU accelerators [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. The Overview section attributes it more specifically to strong demand for 5th generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs [0000002488-26-000018:0070].
Data Center operating income was $3.6 billion in 2025, compared with $3.5 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. The increase was primarily due to higher revenue, partially offset by higher cost of sales, higher operating expenses, and approximately $440 million of net inventory and related charges tied to the U.S. government export control on AMD Instinct MI308 Data Center GPU products [0000002488-26-000018:0077].

questions.question: How did AMD change its segment reporting in fiscal 2025, and what drove the growth of the Client and Gaming segment that year?

answer.text:
Beginning in the first quarter of fiscal 2025, AMD combined its Client and Gaming segments into one reportable segment to align with how it manages its business, and all prior period segment data were retrospectively adjusted [0000002488-26-000018:0006][0000002488-26-000018:0070]. AMD now has three reportable segments: Data Center, Client and Gaming, and Embedded [0000002488-26-000018:0006]. The Client and Gaming businesses are not separate reportable operating segments, but AMD continues to disclose revenue for each separately [0000002488-26-000018:0100].
Client and Gaming net revenue was $14.6 billion in 2025, up 51% from $9.6 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. The filing attributes this growth primarily to strong demand for AMD Ryzen processors, semi-custom game console SoCs and Radeon gaming GPUs [0000002488-26-000018:0070]. Client net revenue of $10.6 billion rose 51% from $7.1 billion, driven by a 31% increase in unit shipments of processors and a 15% increase in average selling price of processors, reflecting strong demand for AMD desktop and mobile Ryzen processors [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. Gaming net revenue of $3.9 billion also rose 51%, from $2.6 billion, driven by higher semi-custom revenue and strong demand for Radeon gaming GPUs [0000002488-26-000018:0077]. Client and Gaming operating income was $2.9 billion in 2025, compared to $1.2 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0077].

OPTIONAL MATCH (f)-[mr:REPORTS]->(m:MetricValue)-[:MEASURES]->(s)

WITH f, s, edge_ids + node_ids + metric_ids AS ids, m
WHERE size(ids) > 0
RETURN f.fiscal_period AS period, s.name AS segment, m.concept AS metric, ids AS chunk_ids
ORDER BY CASE WHEN toLower(s.name) CONTAINS 'client' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, size(ids) DESC

questions.question: What were AMD's main product and AI strategy milestones in 2025, as described in the FY2025 10-K MD&A?

answer.text:
AMD said a priority in 2025 was accelerating growth in the Data Center segment, where demand for its data center AI GPU products was strong as large hyperscale customers, OEMs and ODMs deployed AMD Instinct MI350X Series GPUs [0000002488-26-000018:0071]. It advanced its AMD AI GPU roadmap toward an annual cadence of leadership for AMD Instinct solutions, beginning with the MI350 Series GPUs in 2025 [0000002488-26-000018:0071].
Beyond GPUs, AMD launched the 5th Gen AMD EPYC family of server processors in 2025 [0000002488-26-000018:0071]. It expanded its data center portfolio with new networking solutions, including the AMD Pensando "Pollara" 400 AI NICs and "Vulcano" AI NICs [0000002488-26-000018:0071]. It also previewed its Helios AI rack-scale platform, which incorporates all of its data center products (CPUs, GPUs and networking) [0000002488-26-000018:0071].
In Client and Gaming, AMD brought to market AMD Radeon 9000 Series GPUs and Radeon AI PRO 9700 GPUs based on the AMD RDNA 4 graphics architecture, along with new Ryzen Threadripper 9000 Series processors [0000002488-26-000018:0071]. In its x86 Embedded portfolio, it introduced three new AMD EPYC embedded processor series: EPYC Embedded 9005, 4005 and 2005 [0000002488-26-000018:0071].
AMD also made strategic acquisitions to advance its software capabilities, including compiler and AI expertise, to scale its photonics and co-packaged optics solutions, and to add expertise in high-speed inference and reasoning-based AI technologies [0000002488-26-000018:0071]. It brought in multiple AI teams to develop a comprehensive software ecosystem, and delivered optimizations and expanded framework and library support in the latest version of AMD ROCm software [0000002488-26-000018:0071].
The MD&A also reports that net revenue rose 34% to $34.6 billion in 2025, from $25.8 billion in 2024 [0000002488-26-000018:0070]. Data Center net revenue was $16.6 billion, up 32%, and Client and Gaming net revenue was $14.6 billion, up 51% [0000002488-26-000018:0070].

questions.question: What happened with AMD's acquisition of ZT Systems during fiscal 2025, including the subsequent divestiture of its manufacturing business?

answer.text:
AMD completed the acquisition of ZT Systems on March 31, 2025, for total purchase consideration of $4.4 billion [0000002488-25-000108:0014]. The consideration was $3,188 million of cash paid on the Acquisition Date, $860 million for 8,335,849 shares issued, and $361 million for the fair value of contingent consideration not yet paid, totaling $4,409 million [0000002488-25-000108:0014]. The contingent consideration represented up to 740,961 AMD shares and $300 million of cash, payable to ZT Systems stockholders and warrant holders if the contingencies were fully met [0000002488-25-000108:0014]. Goodwill of $208 million was assigned to the Data Center reporting unit [0000002488-25-000108:0014].
When it announced the deal in August 2024, AMD disclosed its intent to divest ZT Systems' data center infrastructure manufacturing business (the ZT Manufacturing Business) and keep only certain intellectual property and employees (the ZT Design Business) [0000002488-25-000108:0015]. Upon acquisition, the manufacturing business was therefore classified as held for sale and reported in discontinued operations [0000002488-25-000108:0015]. The ZT Design Business results, which are not material, are included in the Data Center segment within continuing operations [0000002488-25-000108:0015].
As of June 28, 2025, the held-for-sale assets totaled $4,326 million and the liabilities totaled $1,968 million [0000002488-25-000108:0015]. questions.question: What caused the declines in AMD's Gaming and Embedded segment revenue in fiscal 2024?

answer.text:
AMD's Gaming net revenue fell 58% to $2.6 billion in 2024, from $6.2 billion in 2023, and the filing says the decrease was primarily due to lower semi-custom product revenue [0000002488-25-000012:0074][0000002488-25-000012:0068].
Embedded net revenue fell 33% to $3.6 billion in 2024, from $5.3 billion in 2023, primarily because of lower demand as customers continued to normalize their inventory levels [0000002488-25-000012:0074].
Customers with higher inventory levels may draw down existing inventory and order less, and Embedded revenue decreased in 2024 as customers continued to normalize inventory [0000002488-25-000012:0025].
In the first quarter of 2024, the filing attributed the Gaming decline to lower semi-custom revenue and lower Radeon GPU sales, and the Embedded decline to customers continuing to manage their inventory levels [0000002488-24-000056:0023].

questions.question: How does AMD's FY2025 10-K describe the status of the AI Diffusion Rule and the risks from potential replacement export rules and tariffs?

answer.text:
AMD's FY2025 10-K says that in January 2025 BIS issued a final rule, commonly referred to as the "AI Diffusion Rule," that would have imposed new restrictions on the export, reexport and in-country transfer of certain advanced semiconductor devices and technology [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. In May 2025, BIS announced its intention to rescind the rule, publish a regulation formalizing the rescission, and issue replacement rules in the future [0000002488-26-000018:0043].
On the replacement rules, AMD says they may limit its ability to engage in certain business transactions, require new export licenses, delay shipments, or necessitate changes in compliance processes and product designs [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. BIS's announced plans also create uncertainty over whether specific products, technologies or software fall within the scope of any new restrictions, and over whether BIS will grant licenses in a timely manner or at all [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. AMD adds that compliance with planned or existing rules could result in increased costs, disruption of key customer and supplier relationships, loss of competitive positioning in international markets or reputational harm [0000002488-26-000018:0043].
On tariffs, AMD says the U.S. government has instituted or proposed changes in trade policies, including higher tariffs on imports into the U.S., which could significantly impact its business, particularly the import of products manufactured outside the U.S. [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. Retaliatory actions by foreign governments could result in tariffs, trade protection measures or other restrictions on AMD's current and future products [0000002488-26-000018:0043]. Customer demand could then decline, which could hurt revenue and result in inventory impairment charges [0000002488-26-000018:0044]. For example, tariffs on hardware required for data centers could raise costs for customers, potentially causing them to delay or cancel AI infrastructure investments [0000002488-26-000018:0044].

questions.question: How did Intel change its approach to deploying manufacturing capital in 2025, and what does its FY2025 10-K say would happen to Intel 14A if it cannot secure a significant external customer?

answer.text:
In 2025 Intel streamlined its footprint to improve operational efficiency and better align capacity with anticipated demand [0000050863-26-000011:0008]. It initiated the consolidation of its Costa Rican assembly and test operations into other facilities, which it expects to complete by the end of 2026 [0000050863-26-000011:0008]. It also slowed the pace of construction for its new Ohio fab and discontinued planned expansions in Germany (fab) and Poland (assembly and test facility) [0000050863-26-000011:0008]. The Costa Rican operations are being consolidated into larger existing sites in Vietnam and Malaysia [0000050863-26-000011:0034]. The filing says these actions better align capital spending with market demand and reflect a focus on deploying capital in coordination with tangible milestones and scaling capacity as needed [0000050863-26-000011:0034]. Intel also says it will deploy capital on new nodes and manufacturing facilities only where it believes they will yield an attractive return [0000050863-26-000011:0034].
If Intel cannot secure a significant external customer for Intel 14A, it announced that it may pause or discontinue its pursuit of Intel 14A and successor leading-edge process technologies [0000050863-26-000011:0008]. The filing says it would then face the prospect that developing and manufacturing Intel 14A and successor nodes would not be economical, and it may also pause or discontinue various manufacturing expansion projects [0000050863-26-000011:0034]. In that event, Intel would expect over time to shift manufacturing to third-party foundries, particularly TSMC, as it develops products for nodes beyond Intel 18A and Intel 18A-P [0000050863-26-000011:0008]. Intel would expect a majority of its products to continue to be manufactured in its own facilities, using nodes up to Intel 18A-P, through at least 2030 [0000050863-26-000011:0034]. The filing adds that Intel has been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of its nodes, and that its prospects for securing one for Intel 14A are uncertain [0000050863-26-000011:0065].

questions.question: What were the key terms of Intel's August 2025 agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce, as described in its FY2025 10-K?

answer.text:
On August 22, 2025, Intel entered into a Warrant and Common Stock Agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC) to support the continued expansion of U.S. semiconductor technology and manufacturing leadership [0000050863-26-000011:0030].
Under the agreement, the U.S. government agreed to make disbursements consisting of $5.7 billion from the acceleration of certain disbursements under an amendment to the November 2024 Direct Funding Agreement under the CHIPS Act, plus $3.2 billion of disbursements under the Secure Enclave program, to be made as Intel performs on its commitments [0000050863-26-000011:0127].
As compensation, Intel agreed to issue to the DOC up to 433 million shares of common stock, of which 275 million would be issued on the closing date and 159 million would be issued into escrow to be released as Secure Enclave disbursements are received [0000050863-26-000011:0127]. Intel also agreed to issue warrants to purchase up to 241 million shares at $20.00 per share if it were to cease to directly or indirectly own at least 51% of its foundry business [0000050863-26-000011:0127].
The DOC also agreed that, to the maximum extent permissible under applicable law, Intel's obligations under the DFA would be considered discharged, other than with respect to Secure Enclave [0000050863-26-000011:0127].
On that date Intel and the DOC amended the DFA to remove the prior project milestone requirements and certain other conditions to disbursements, Intel received the remaining $5.7 billion of DFA disbursements, and it issued the 275 million shares, the warrants and the 159 million escrowed shares [0000050863-26-000011:0127]. The amendment also removed substantially all other requirements under the agreement other than those required by law, including those tied to the $2.3 billion previously received and recognized as government incentives [0000050863-26-000011:0030].
The escrowed shares are released to the U.S. government on a $20.00 per share basis as Intel receives the $3.2 billion of Secure Enclave disbursements, and 3 million had been released as of December 27, 2025 [0000050863-26-000011:0030]. Secure Enclave proceeds received after the agreement's effective date are attributed as equity and are not subject to Intel's grant accounting policy [0000050863-26-000011:0133].
Intel's accounting conclusion for the agreement was adjusted after consultation with the SEC staff, which concluded in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, and Intel concluded the adjustments were immaterial to its Q3 2025 Form 10-Q financial statements [0000050863-26-000011:0030]. In 2025, interest and other, net, included a $1.8 billion net loss from the change in fair value of the derivative liability for the Escrowed Shares [0000050863-26-000011:0046].

questions.question: What did Intel's 2025 Restructuring Plan aim to do, and what restructuring and related charges did Intel record in 2025?

answer.text:
Intel's 2025 Restructuring Plan was implemented to lower expenses, streamline the organizational structure and reduce management layers across functions, while reallocating resources toward the core client and server businesses by reducing investment in lower-priority programs and initiatives [0000050863-26-000011:0032]. These headcount reductions cut Intel's core workforce by approximately 15% by the end of fiscal 2025, compared with the Q2 2025 ending headcount [0000050863-26-000011:0032].
In 2025, Intel recognized restructuring charges of $2.2 billion, consisting primarily of charges from initiating and deploying the 2025 Restructuring Plan and from substantially completing the 2024 Restructuring Plan [0000050863-26-000011:0032]. Of this, cash-based employee severance and related employee exit charges were $1.8 billion, and non-cash asset impairment charges were $474 million, resulting from the exit of certain non-core lines of business and the consolidation and exit of certain real estate properties [0000050863-26-000011:0032].
The restructuring and other charges table shows fiscal 2025 totals of $2,191 million, made up of $1,790 million of employee severance and benefit arrangements, $(121) million of litigation charges and other, and $522 million of asset impairment charges [0000050863-26-000011:0044]. The employee severance line includes net charges of $1.5 billion for the 2025 Restructuring Plan and $281 million for the 2024 Restructuring Plan and other actions [0000050863-26-000011:0044]. The $522 million of asset impairment charges consisted primarily of non-cash charges associated with the 2025 Restructuring Plan [0000050863-26-000011:0044]. The cumulative cost of the 2025 Restructuring Plan as of December 27, 2025 was $2.0 billion, and Intel expects total charges of approximately $2.2 billion under the plan [0000050863-26-000011:0135].
Separately, Intel recorded non-cash charges of $950 million, net of certain items, to cost of sales in 2025 for accelerated depreciation and impairment of certain manufacturing assets that were determined to have no remaining operational use, which affected the Intel Foundry segment [0000050863-26-000011:0032].

questions.question: How did Intel describe Intel Foundry's strategy, process technology offerings and competitors in its FY2024 10-K?

answer.text:
Intel said Intel Foundry, which comprises technology development, manufacturing and foundry services, seeks to deliver the best systems foundry capabilities to support Intel Products and external customers [0000050863-25-000009:0030].
On strategy, Intel said it expects its manufacturing facilities to continue to mostly produce its own products for many years, while aiming to become a major provider of semiconductor manufacturing solutions for third parties as well [0000050863-25-000009:0030]. It said volume from its own products provides the scale required for leading-edge foundry operations and helps derisk the offerings for third-party customers [0000050863-25-000009:0030]. Third-party customers would add scale on the leading edge and, for mature nodes, allow better monetization of technology and manufacturing facility investments [0000050863-25-000009:0030]. Intel also plans to create greater independence for its foundry operations by establishing Intel Foundry as an independent subsidiary, which it expects to give clearer separation for foundry customers and suppliers and more flexibility to evaluate separate sources of funding and capital structures [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. Intel said it believes it is currently one of only three manufacturers pursuing 2nm lithography [0000050863-25-000009:0030].
On process technology, Intel said it expects to achieve volume production on its 2nm node, Intel 18A, in 2025 [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. The process technologies available to external customers are expected to include Intel 18A, featuring RibbonFET (gate-all-around) and PowerVia (back-side power delivery) as expected industry firsts [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. They also include the new Intel 3 process using EUV lithography, the established Intel 7 and Intel 16 processes, and a new 12nm process being developed in collaboration with UMC [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. Intel also announced an extension of its roadmap beyond Intel 18A with Intel 14A [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. Its advanced assembly and test offerings include technologies for packaging single chips or combining multiple chips adjacent to each other, stacked, or both [0000050863-25-000009:0031].
On competitors, Intel said Intel Foundry's competitors are primarily semiconductor foundries focused on wafers and packaging technologies from fabrication plants based primarily in Asia, including TSMC, Samsung, Global Foundries, UMC and SMIC [0000050863-25-000009:0031]. It said it competes with TSMC and Samsung in the advanced process technology marketplace [0000050863-25-000009:0031].

questions.question: Where does the European Commission competition case against Intel stand in its FY2025 10-K, and how much has Intel accrued for it?

answer.text:
In 2009 the EC found that Intel had used unfair business practices, and it imposed a €1.1 billion fine, which Intel paid in the third quarter of 2009 [0000050863-26-000011:0171]. In January 2022 the General Court annulled the EC's 2009 findings on rebates and the €1.1 billion fine, which was returned to Intel in February 2022 [0000050863-26-000011:0171]. The General Court did not annul the 2009 finding that Intel made payments to prevent sales of specific rival products [0000050863-26-000011:0171]. In October 2024 the Court of Justice dismissed the EC's appeal on rebates, which upheld the General Court's judgment [0000050863-26-000011:0171].
In September 2023 the EC imposed a €376 million ($401 million) fine based on the finding about payments to prevent sales of rival products [0000050863-26-000011:0172]. Intel appealed, and in December 2025 the General Court reduced the fine to €237 million ($277 million) [0000050863-26-000011:0172]. Intel may appeal that decision to the Court of Justice [0000050863-26-000011:0172].
As of December 27, 2025, Intel had accrued approximately $311 million for the fine, including foreign currency revaluation effects and accrued interest [0000050863-26-000011:0172][0000050863-26-000011:0171]. Intel says it cannot reasonably estimate any potential loss in excess of that amount, given the procedural posture and nature of the proceedings [0000050863-26-000011:0172]. In 2025 Intel recorded a $163 million benefit from reducing the previously accrued $401 million fine [0000050863-26-000011:0049]. The fine remains unpaid on appeal, its payment is guaranteed by a third party, and Intel funded that guarantee in 2025 by depositing $340 million in legally restricted accounts [0000050863-26-000011:0049][0000050863-26-000011:0136].
